title: The width that moved the work

narration.essentials: Cycle 0, and the whole program fits in a breath: two branches, two constants, an exit. Five instructions — and the ISSUE control changes how long they take without changing one thing they do.
narration.detailed: You met `paired-branches` in "One branch unit": `bne x0, x0, done` twice in a row, then `li a0, 42`, then the exit. Neither branch is taken — x0 is not different from itself — so nothing is ever flushed, and no instruction in this program reads a register another one writes. That makes it the cleanest width experiment in the corpus: no speculation to recover from, no memory to wait on, no dependence to forward. Everything the ISSUE control can possibly change here is which instructions travel together. Two wide, this run takes 7 cycles. One wide, 9. The next three steps ask what the other two slots are worth.
narration.expert: Fetch takes as many instructions per cycle as the machine is wide, so cycle 0 already differs by width: two wide it holds the two `bne`s, four wide it holds those two plus `li a0, 42` and `li a7, 10`. Fetching is not issuing, though — the group is formed one stage later, in decode, and this program's entire width story happens there. Five instructions, five fetches, no flush at any width, and not one register dependence between any two of them. Everything that usually competes with the extra slots has been taken out of the way, which is why this program can answer the question the other two width lessons could only answer around the edges of a loop.

narration.essentials: The younger branch is refused — one branch unit, two control transfers. This is the same refusal at two, three and four wide: widening a machine never gives it a second branch unit.
narration.detailed: "One branch unit" told you what this refusal is: both branches are fetched side by side, neither needs anything the other computes, and the machine still cannot issue them together, because there is exactly one place a control transfer can be resolved. What is new here is that the refusal does not move. Two wide, this run holds exactly one `branch-slot` refusal. Three wide, one. Four wide, one — the same one, in the same cycle, against the same instruction. Extra slots do not replicate the branch unit; all they do is make the group behind the branch bigger. And look at which way the count runs against the clock. One wide, this program is refused nothing at all and takes 9 cycles. Four wide, it is refused once and takes 6. A refusal is not a fine the machine pays.
narration.expert: Count the refusals at each width and the row reads 0, 1, 1, 1 — One wide, 0, because a group of one has no younger member to refuse; Two wide, 1; Three wide, 1; Four wide, 1. Put the cycle counts under that row and it reads 9, 7, 7, 6. The two rows do not line up at either end, and no reading of the first as a cost survives the second. The pinning is structural rather than lucky: `branch-slot` fires when a candidate group holds two control transfers, this program has exactly one adjacent pair of them, and the branch unit stayed single at every width the control offers. `intra-pair-raw` would climb with the width on a program full of dependences — "Four in a row" goes 6, 13, 12 — but `branch-slot` cannot climb, because the hardware it names was never replicated.

narration.essentials: The elder branch resolves: not taken. Nothing is flushed and nothing is re-fetched, so from here on the only thing width can change is which instructions share a cycle. Set the ISSUE control to 3 and run the program again.
narration.detailed: `bne x0, x0, done` compares x0 with itself, finds them equal, and falls through. The machine had predicted not-taken and kept fetching straight ahead, so it guessed right and there is nothing to undo: no flush, no re-fetch, no discarded work anywhere in this run at any width. That is what makes the next two steps readable. In "Where widening stops paying" the extra slots were competing with a mispredict shadow, and in "Four in a row" with a dependence chain; here there is neither. The younger `bne` and the three instructions behind it — `li a0, 42`, `li a7, 10`, `ecall` — are all the material width has to work with, and nothing in that set needs anything from the rest of it. Two wide, they do not all fit in one group. Set the ISSUE control to 3 and run the program again, then step back to here.
narration.expert: A not-taken branch under a not-taken prediction is the one control transfer that costs nothing: `branch-resolved` reports `predicted=false, actual=false`, no `flush` is emitted, and the fetch stream never turns around. Both branches in this program are that. So the flush bill — which set the per-pass cost in both of the other width lessons and was width-invariant in both — is zero here, at every width, and the run's length is nothing but its issue-group count plus the 4 cycles of the pipeline's own fill and drain — the same 4 at one, two, three and four slots. Subtract them and what is left is a pure measurement of how the decode stage partitions five instructions. Set the ISSUE control to 3 and run it again.

narration.essentials: `li a7, 10` executes — Two wide in cycle 4, Three wide in cycle 3. The third slot was used: the group the younger branch leads grew from 2 instructions to 3. And the run did not get shorter for it — Two wide, 7 cycles; Three wide, 7 cycles. Now set the ISSUE control to 4.
narration.detailed: This is the step the lesson exists for. Two wide, the machine forms three issue groups: the elder `bne` alone, then the younger `bne` with `li a0, 42`, then `li a7, 10` with `ecall`. Three wide, it forms three issue groups again — but not the same three. The younger `bne` now leads a group of 3: itself, `li a0` and `li a7`. So the third slot was not idle hardware, the way it was in "Where widening stops paying". It was filled, and `li a7, 10` executes a cycle earlier for it — cycle 3 rather than cycle 4. What it did not do is remove a group. Pulling `li a7` forward pushed `ecall` out of the last group and into one of its own, so three groups became three groups — Two wide, 7 cycles; Three wide, 7 cycles. The widening moved the work; it did not shorten the run. Now set the ISSUE control to 4 and come back to this same instruction.
narration.expert: The group the younger branch leads is exactly as wide as the machine: Two wide it holds 2 instructions, Three wide 3, Four wide 4. That is about the cleanest statement of what an issue slot is that the corpus can produce, and it is only true because this program hands the decode stage four adjacent instructions with no dependence among them and only one of them a control transfer. But a run's length tracks the NUMBER of groups, not their size, and going from two slots to three repartitions the same five instructions into the same three parts: `[bne][bne, li a0][li a7, ecall]` becomes `[bne][bne, li a0, li a7][ecall]`. Three parts either way. Only a partition with fewer parts is worth a cycle, and a slot that fills is no evidence it produced one — which is the trap this whole track keeps resetting, met here on the group table instead of on a refusal count. Set the ISSUE control to 4, which does produce one.

narration.essentials: The last instruction retires. Four wide, the whole run is 2 issue groups and 6 cycles — the younger branch, both constants and the exit all issued together. One wide it was 9 cycles, Two wide 7, Three wide 7.
narration.detailed: `ecall` retires and the program is done, with 42 in `a0` — the same 42 at one, two, three and four slots, because width has never once changed what a program computes. What it changed is the partition. One wide, 5 issue groups and 9 cycles: every instruction alone. Two wide, 3 groups and 7 cycles. Three wide, 3 groups and 7 cycles — the slot filled, the count did not fall. Four wide, 2 groups and 6 cycles: the younger `bne`, `li a0, 42`, `li a7, 10` and `ecall` all issue in one cycle, and the group that used to hold the tail is simply gone. Read the group counts down that list — 5, 3, 3, 2 — then the cycle counts — 9, 7, 7, 6. They step down together, and they step down in the same two places. On this program the question "what is another slot worth?" has exactly one honest form: does it remove a group?
narration.expert: The strongest fact in this lesson is one the trace cannot show you. Record this program at two, three and four wide and the three event lists are the same list — every event, every payload, every instruction id, the same number of times: 5 fetches, 5 retires, 1 refusal, 2 branch resolutions, 0 flushes, at all three widths. Nothing is added and nothing is taken away. Only the cycle each event lands in differs, and that difference is worth a cycle of the six. So a width change on this program is invisible to any check that asks WHAT the machine did and visible only to one that asks WHEN. It does not generalize, and the other two lessons in this track are the proof: "Four in a row" gains two forwards at four slots that exist at no narrower width, because widening a machine with dependences in it changes which values are ready when. Two programs, two channels, and neither one subsumes the other.
